questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A currency-union member under a price shock
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a price shock affects a currency-union member
questions.stem: Item 0001: a currency-union member faces a price shock; what is the main effect?

options.text: A price shock hurts members that cannot adjust their exchange rate.
Members can devalue instantly to restore competitiveness.
Price shocks only affect non-union members.
options.misconception: excludes union members from price shocks

options.text: Inflation differences disappear automatically in a union.

questions.explanation: A member sharing a currency cannot devalue to absorb a shock, so adjustment must come through prices, wages, or fiscal policy. The shock still matters.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: The assumption a geopolitical theory rests on
questions.learningObjective: Identify the assumption behind a geopolitical theory
questions.stem: Item 0002: a theory claims location shapes power; what assumption does it rest on?

options.text: The theory assumes technology erases distance.
The theory assumes geography shapes political power.
The theory assumes all states are democratic.
options.misconception: adds regime assumption not in theory

options.text: The theory assumes population is evenly spread.

questions.explanation: Geopolitical theories start from the idea that location and spatial relationships influence power. Technology, regime type, or even population spread are not the core assumption.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: The claim built on a heartland
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a heartland claim rests on
questions.stem: Item 0003: a theorist claims a central landmass is decisive; what is that claim built on?

answer.exemplar: The heartland claim rests on control of a central landmass, arguing that interior resources and strategic depth can dominate surrounding regions.

questions.explanation: The heartland idea centres on controlling an interior landmass with resources and strategic depth. It is not primarily about naval power or democratic institutions.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why a rimland is claimed to matter more than its size
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a rimland is claimed to matter more than its size
questions.stem: Item 0004: a rimland has 20 percent of the land area but 60 percent of the coastline; compute the coastline-to-area ratio.
questions.explanation: Divide 60 percent by 20 percent to get 3. The rimland claim stresses coastal access disproportionate to its land area.
questions.hint: Divide coastline share by area share.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Transits and tonnage through a strait
questions.learningObjective: Explain what strait tonnage indicates

stimulus.body: A train dispatcher's log records 12 million tons of cargo passing through a strait in one month. Military vessels account for a small share of that tonnage.

questions.stem: Item 0005: what does this tonnage mainly indicate?

options.text: It measures land border crossings.
options.misconception: confuses maritime strait with land border

options.text: It measures only military ships.
Tonnage through a strait measures transit volume and strategic value.
It is unrelated to trade routes.
options.misconception: ignores link between tonnage and trade

questions.explanation: High cargo tonnage signals heavy transit use and strategic importance for trade routes. Military tonnage is only a small part of the total.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Correcting an overvaluation inside a currency union
questions.learningObjective: Explain how overvaluation is corrected inside a currency union
questions.stem: Item 0006: a member's real exchange rate is overvalued inside a currency union; how is it corrected?

options.text: Members can devalue their shared currency unilaterally.
Overvaluation corrects itself without policy.
Fiscal transfers are the only possible tool.
options.misconception: overstates fiscal transfers as sole tool

options.text: Correction requires internal price and wage adjustment.

questions.explanation: Without a national currency, realignment must occur through internal price and wage adjustment, possibly aided by fiscal transfers. It is not automatic or unilateral.
questions.hint: Internal prices and wages must adjust.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: The objections to a heartland claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain objections to a heartland claim
questions.stem: Item 0007: critics challenge a heartland claim; what is their main objection?

options.text: Critics say the heartland has no resources.
Critics say technology and air power reduce heartland dominance.
Critics say sea power is irrelevant.
Critics say geography never matters.

questions.explanation: Critics argue technology, air power, and mobility reduce the decisive advantage of an interior heartland. They do not usually deny resources or claim geography is irrelevant.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Testing an irredentist claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an irredentist claim asserts
questions.stem: Item 0008: a state claims territory across a border; what does that claim assert?

options.text: It asserts only economic zones matter.
It asserts all borders are permanently fixed.
An irredentist claim asserts territory belongs to a nation beyond borders.
It asserts no minority exists in the territory.

questions.explanation: Irredentism claims that territory inhabited by a nation should be incorporated into its state, even across current borders. It is not about fixed borders or economics alone.
